note: This stage spans TWO book chapters in the 10th edition. Evolution, the Intel x86 line and ARM are ch 1; the performance material is ch 2. `pnpm book:map` owns that mapping and reports 10 of 18 chapters renumbered. The six P items here carry no stem of their own — resolve.ts takes it from the solver.

items.stem: The first generation of computers used which technology for its digital logic elements and memory?
distractors: Discrete transistors
Small-scale integrated circuits
Electromechanical relays
items.rationale: First generation is vacuum tubes, second is transistors, third is integrated circuits. Relays predate the generations scheme entirely and belong to the electromechanical machines that came before ENIAC.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.3 — The First Generation: Vacuum Tubes

items.stem: Put these computer generations in the order they appeared.
items.rationale: Each generation is defined by the logic technology of its day, and each is smaller, faster and cheaper than the one before. The progression is the physical story behind Moore's law: the same functions realised in progressively less silicon.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.3 — the generation headings

items.stem: What is the fundamental design approach first implemented in the IAS computer, which makes it the prototype of all later general-purpose machines?
items.correct: The stored-program concept — instructions and data share one memory
distractors: The use of vacuum tubes rather than relays for logic
The separation of instruction memory from data memory
The use of an accumulator for arithmetic results
items.rationale: The stored-program concept, attributed to von Neumann and developed independently by Turing, is what lets a machine be reprogrammed rather than rewired. The second distractor describes a Harvard architecture, which is the opposite arrangement.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.3 — the IAS computer and the stored-program concept

items.stem: Which contemporary processor technique is defined as the ability to issue more than one instruction in every clock cycle?
distractors: Pipelining
Speculative execution
Branch prediction
items.rationale: Superscalar uses multiple parallel pipelines to issue several instructions per cycle. Pipelining overlaps the STAGES of instructions without issuing more than one per cycle, which is the distinction this item exists to draw.
items.source: ch-02.md §2.1 — techniques built into contemporary processors

items.stem: What does data flow analysis allow a processor to do?
items.correct: Schedule instructions to execute when their operands are ready, independent of program order
distractors: Predict which branch of the code will be taken next
Execute instructions ahead of their appearance and hold the results temporarily
Retrieve more bits from memory in a single access
items.rationale: Data flow analysis works out which instructions depend on which results, so an optimised schedule can be built. The second distractor is speculative execution, which USES data flow analysis but is a different technique.
items.source: ch-02.md §2.1 — data flow analysis

items.stem: Why does branch prediction increase performance even though it does not make any single instruction faster?
items.correct: It increases the amount of work available to execute by prefetching and buffering the likely instructions
distractors: It removes branches from the instruction stream entirely
It reduces the number of cycles each branch instruction takes
It allows two branches to be taken simultaneously
items.rationale: The processor's raw speed is wasted unless it is fed a constant stream of work. Prediction keeps the pipeline full by guessing what comes next. Branches are not removed and their individual cost is unchanged; what changes is whether the processor has anything to do while they resolve.
items.source: ch-02.md §2.1 — branch prediction, and 'feeding the monster'
ch-02.md §2.3 — Amdahl's Law

items.stem: Which Intel processor is the first appearance of the x86 architecture?
items.rationale: The 8086 is a 16-bit machine and the first x86. The 8080 came earlier and was the world's first general-purpose microprocessor, but it is 8-bit and pre-x86 — which is why its number looks similar and it is the distractor most often chosen.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.4 — 'The 8086 is the first appearance of the x86 architecture'

items.stem: Which Intel x86 processor was the first 32-bit machine and the first to support multitasking?
distractors: Pentium
items.rationale: The 80286 extended addressing to 16 MB but remained 16-bit. The 80386 was the 32-bit overhaul. The 80486 added sophisticated cache, instruction pipelining and a built-in math coprocessor, and the Pentium added superscalar execution.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.4 — the 80386 entry

items.stem: The Pentium Pro deepened the superscalar organization begun with the Pentium. Which group of techniques did it use aggressively?
items.correct: Register renaming, branch prediction, data flow analysis and speculative execution
distractors: MMX multimedia instructions and a built-in math coprocessor
Streaming SIMD Extensions and dual-core execution
Instruction pipelining and an on-chip instruction queue
items.rationale: Those four are exactly the techniques §2.1 lists for keeping a fast processor fed, and the Pentium Pro is where they arrive together. MMX is the Pentium II, SSE is the Pentium III, and dual core is the Core.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.4 — the Pentium Pro entry

items.stem: What is unusual about ARM Holdings' business model?
items.correct: It does not manufacture processors; it designs architectures and licenses them to manufacturers
distractors: It manufactures every ARM chip itself and sells no designs
It sells only completed devices, never the processors inside them
It licenses only software, and the hardware designs are public domain
items.rationale: ARM Holdings licenses two kinds of product: a processor, where the customer uses ARM's design in their own chip, and a processor architecture, where the customer designs their own compliant processor. This is why ARM cores appear in chips from many different manufacturers.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — ARM Evolution and the two licensable products

items.stem: ARM is a family of processors built on which design philosophy?
distractors: CISC — complex instruction set computing, like the x86
VLIW — very long instruction word
Stack-based execution with no general-purpose registers
items.rationale: Stallings uses exactly two running examples: the x86 as the CISC exemplar and ARM as the RISC one. Keeping that pairing straight matters, because most later chapters compare the two.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.4 intro — the CISC/RISC pairing, and §1.6

items.stem: What is regular about the ARM instruction set that makes it efficient to implement across a wide range of products?
items.correct: All instructions are 32 bits long and follow a regular format
distractors: Instructions vary in length so common operations can be encoded compactly
All instructions are 16 bits long to save memory in embedded devices
Instructions are decoded into microinstructions of a fixed internal width
items.rationale: Fixed-width, regularly formatted instructions are a defining RISC trait: decoding is simple and predictable, which is what makes pipelining straightforward. The first distractor describes CISC encoding, which is the x86's approach.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — Instruction Set Architecture

items.stem: Which ARM Cortex family is intended for application processors in devices such as smartphones and eBook readers?
distractors: Cortex-R
Cortex-M
Cortex-M0+
items.rationale: The three Cortex architectures are labelled with the initials A, R and M: A for application, R for real-time, M for microcontroller. The Cortex-A runs above 1 GHz and supports an MMU, which full operating systems like Linux and Android require.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — ARM Products, Cortex-A/Cortex-A50

items.stem: Automotive braking systems, mass storage controllers and printing devices are given as examples of embedded systems that would use which ARM family?
distractors: Cortex-A
Cortex-M
Cortex-A50
items.rationale: The Cortex-R is built for real-time applications, where the timing of events must be controlled with rapid response. Those three examples are the book's own. A braking system's requirement is not raw throughput but a bounded, predictable response latency.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — Cortex-R examples

items.stem: The Cortex-M series was developed primarily for which domain?
items.correct: Microcontrollers, where deterministic interrupt management, low gate count and lowest possible power matter most
distractors: Mobile application processors running full operating systems
Server-class processors for cloud data centres
Real-time industrial controllers requiring a memory protection unit only
items.rationale: Cortex-M targets the microcontroller domain — IoT devices, wireless sensor and actuator networks, automotive body electronics. The last distractor describes the Cortex-R, which is the neighbouring family and the easiest one to confuse it with.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — Cortex-M

items.stem: Which ARM Cortex family includes a memory management unit (MMU), and what does that enable?
items.correct: Cortex-A — an MMU translates virtual addresses to physical ones, which full operating systems require
distractors: Cortex-R — an MMU stops one program accessing another's memory
Cortex-M — an MMU reduces interrupt latency
All three, since every ARM core supports virtual memory
items.rationale: Only the Cortex-A has an MMU. The Cortex-R and Cortex-M have a memory PROTECTION unit instead, which fences programs off from each other but does not translate addresses. The first distractor describes what an MPU does while naming the MMU.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — MMU on Cortex-A, MPU on Cortex-R and Cortex-M

items.stem: Most Cortex-R processors have no MMU. What justifies leaving it out?
items.correct: Limited data requirements and few simultaneous processes remove the need for virtual memory support
distractors: An MMU cannot operate at the clock frequencies the Cortex-R targets
Real-time code is written in assembly, which does not use virtual addresses
The MPU already performs address translation more quickly
items.rationale: The book's reason is workload, not capability: with limited data and a small number of concurrent processes, the elaborate hardware and software support virtual memory needs would buy nothing. Note the last distractor's claim is false — an MPU does not translate addresses at all.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — 'the limited data requirements and the limited number of simultaneous processes'

items.stem: Which Cortex family uses ONLY the Thumb-2 instruction set rather than both ARM and Thumb-2?
distractors: Cortex-A
Cortex-A50
Cortex-R
items.rationale: The Cortex-A and Cortex-A50 use both the ARM and Thumb-2 instruction sets. The Cortex-M uses Thumb-2 alone, which suits a family optimised for the smallest possible gate count and power draw.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.6 — 'The Cortex-M uses only the Thumb-2 instruction set'
